name: Bhindi Masala
cuisine: North Indian (Punjabi and everyday home-style dry/semi-dry sabzi, cooked all over India)

ingredients.name: Okra (bhindi / lady's finger)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 18–20 medium pods, sliced into 1.5–2 cm pieces

ingredients.name: Sunflower oil (or groundnut / mustard oil)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 2 tsp (split: 1½ tsp for the okra, ½ tsp for the masala)

ingredients.name: Ginger (adrak)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ¾ tsp, finely chopped or grated

equipment: Wide frying pan or kadai (9–10 inch), preferably non-stick or well-seasoned iron
Chopping board and knife (both completely dry)
Colander or strainer, and a clean dry kitchen towel (or newspaper / paper towels) for drying the okra
A plate to keep the fried okra aside
Measuring spoons (normal teaspoons are a fine stand-in)
Small bowl for the powdered spices
No lid is needed (this version is cooked uncovered)

steps.title: Wash the okra whole
steps.text: Put the 200 g okra pods in a colander and rinse under running water, rubbing each pod lightly with your fingers. Do not cut them yet.
steps.tip: Wash before cutting, never after. Water inside cut okra is the main cause of sliminess.
steps.visualCue: Pods look clean and bright green, no dust in the ridges.
steps.cameraCheck: The washed okra in the colander
steps.videoShot: Water running over okra pods in a colander.

steps.title: Dry the okra completely
steps.text: Spread the pods on a dry kitchen towel and rub them dry, then leave them spread out for a few minutes (or under a fan) until no damp spots remain.
steps.tip: Many cooks wash the okra in the morning and let it air-dry for hours. Even 10 minutes under a fan helps a lot.
steps.visualCue: Pods feel completely dry to the touch, including the ridges and the tip.
steps.cameraCheck: The dry pods spread on the towel
steps.videoShot: Hands rolling okra pods in a towel.

steps.title: Trim and slice the okra
steps.text: With a dry knife on a dry board, cut off the stem top and the very tip of each pod, then slice into 1.5–2 cm pieces.
steps.tip: Wipe the knife with a dry cloth if it gets sticky. Larger pieces release less slime than thin rounds. If a pod is hard and woody when you cut it, throw that pod away.
steps.visualCue: Even, thumb-width pieces; you may see a few sticky threads on the knife (normal).
steps.cameraCheck: The heap of sliced okra on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife slicing okra into rounds.

steps.title: Slice and chop the aromatics
steps.text: Thinly slice the onion (60 g). Finely chop the tomato (60 g), ginger (¾ tsp), garlic (1 clove), and slit the green chilli.
steps.visualCue: Thin onion slices; tomato in small dice.
steps.cameraCheck: Small heaps of onion, tomato, ginger-garlic and chilli on the board
steps.videoShot: Overhead shot of the chopped heaps.

steps.title: Mix the powdered spices
steps.text: In a small bowl, put ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder. Keep the amchur, garam masala and salt aside separately for the end.
steps.visualCue: A small mound of yellow, red and brown powders.
steps.cameraCheck: The spice bowl, with amchur, garam masala and salt kept separately
steps.videoShot: The powders being spooned into a bowl.

steps.title: Heat the pan with oil for the okra
steps.text: Put the wide pan on medium heat and add 1½ tsp of the oil. Tilt to spread it.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers and flows easily across the pan.
steps.videoShot: Oil spreading across a wide pan.

steps.title: Add the okra in a single layer
steps.text: Add all the sliced okra and spread it out with the spatula so most pieces touch the pan.
steps.tip: Do not add salt now. Salt draws out moisture and makes the okra slimy.
steps.visualCue: A gentle sizzle as the okra hits the pan.
steps.cameraCheck: The okra spread out in the pan
steps.videoShot: Okra pieces tumbling into the pan and being spread out.

steps.title: Pan-fry the okra, uncovered, stirring rarely
steps.text: Cook on medium heat, stirring gently only every 1½–2 minutes.
steps.tip: Never cover the pan, and never add water. Too much stirring breaks the pieces and spreads the slime. Lower the heat a little if the okra browns too fast before the threads are gone.
steps.visualCue: At first the okra looks sticky with white threads; keep going until the threads disappear, the pieces look dry, slightly shrunk and have light golden-brown spots.
steps.cameraCheck: A close-up of the okra pieces showing no sticky threads
steps.videoShot: The spatula lifting dry, lightly browned okra.

steps.title: Check that the okra is cooked
steps.text: Press a piece with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: It is tender and squashes easily but still holds its shape; no sticky strands when you lift the spatula.
steps.cameraCheck: A piece of okra pressed with the spatula
steps.videoShot: The spatula pressing a piece of okra.

steps.title: Move the okra to a plate
steps.text: Tip the cooked okra onto a plate and keep it uncovered.
steps.tip: Leave it uncovered so steam does not soften it again.
steps.visualCue: Dry, separate pieces on the plate.
steps.videoShot: Okra sliding off the pan onto a plate.

steps.title: Temper the cumin
steps.text: In the same pan on medium heat, add the remaining ½ tsp oil, then ½ tsp cumin seeds and the pinch of hing.
steps.tip: The pan already has a little oil left from the okra, so this small amount is enough.
steps.visualCue: The cumin sizzles, darkens one shade and smells toasty.
steps.cameraCheck: The cumin sizzling in the pan
steps.videoShot: Cumin seeds crackling in a little oil.

steps.title: Fry the onion
steps.text: Add the sliced onion and stir on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: The onion turns soft and light golden at the edges.
steps.videoShot: The spatula stirring onions turning golden.

steps.title: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli
steps.visualCue: The raw garlic smell goes and the pan smells fragrant.
steps.cameraCheck: The onion with ginger, garlic and chilli

steps.title: Add the tomato and the spice powders
steps.text: Add the chopped tomato and the spice bowl (turmeric, chilli, coriander powder). Turn the heat to low-medium and stir.
steps.tip: If the masala sticks, press the tomato down harder to release its juice instead of adding water. If you must, add only 1 tsp water.
steps.visualCue: The tomato breaks down into a thick, jammy masala and a little oil shines at the edges.
steps.videoShot: Tomato and spices being mashed with the spatula into a paste.

steps.title: Return the okra to the pan
steps.text: Add the fried okra and toss gently so every piece is coated in masala.
steps.visualCue: The okra is evenly coated in a red-brown masala; no liquid in the pan.
steps.cameraCheck: The okra mixed with the masala
steps.videoShot: The okra being folded into the masala.

steps.title: Add salt and finishing spices, cook briefly
steps.text: Sprinkle ⅓ tsp salt, ½ tsp amchur and ¼ tsp garam masala. Toss gently and cook uncovered on low heat.
steps.tip: Salt and the sour amchur go in last, when the okra is already cooked, so they flavour it without making it slimy.
steps.visualCue: The sabzi looks dry and glossy and smells tangy and spiced.
steps.cameraCheck: The finished sabzi in the pan
steps.videoShot: Amchur and garam masala being sprinkled over the okra.

steps.title: Garnish and serve
steps.text: Switch off the heat, scatter the chopped coriander leaves, taste a piece and adjust salt or amchur. Spoon into a bowl.
steps.visualCue: A dry/semi-dry bowl of okra pieces coated in masala, with soft onions and green flecks.
steps.videoShot: Bhindi masala spooned into a bowl next to a hot roti.

reasons: a vegetable-only dish with 2 tsp oil, no cream, no deep-frying and about 9–10 g of fibre per bowl, plus folate, vitamin K and magnesium from the okra. Points come off because protein is low (about 6 g), so it needs dal, curd, paneer or chana alongside, and okra soaks up oil easily. Restaurant versions often deep-fry the okra before tossing it in masala and use more salt and oil or butter.

researchRating.basis: one of India's most-cooked everyday sabzis and a staple on Punjabi restaurant menus. Recipes are well reviewed (Cook With Manali's bhindi masala 4.97/5 from 87 votes with 9+ comment pages; Archana's Kitchen bhindi masala curry with 3,422 ratings; Green Bowl 2 Soul 4.88/5 from 16 votes; Vegan Richa 4.84/5 from 12 votes; Subbu's Kitchen 4.80/5). Deduction because okra is polarising: many people dislike its sliminess, and almost every recipe has to spend a paragraph on avoiding it.

storage: Refrigerate in an airtight box within 2 hours of cooking. It keeps for 1–2 days in the fridge; it softens and loses its crispness after that. Freezing is not recommended; okra turns mushy and slimy when thawed. To reheat, warm it in a dry pan on medium heat for 2–3 min, tossing gently and uncovered (this brings back some crispness), or microwave uncovered for 1 min. Do not add water.
leftoverRemix: Bhindi masala wrap with curd dip. Warm 1 cup leftover bhindi masala in a pan until it crisps a little, roll it into a roti or paratha with a few raw onion rings and a spoon of hung curd mixed with a pinch of chaat masala and mint. Or crumble it into a bowl of curd with roasted cumin for a quick bhindi raita.
burnOff: about 2.9 km of running (205 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 4.1 km of brisk walking (about 50 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). This is for the sabzi alone; 2 phulkas would add about 2–2.5 km of running.

navratri.reason: skip onion, garlic, hing, turmeric and coriander powder and use sendha namak, cumin, ginger, green chilli and tomato only; okra is not a grain or pulse, but it is not on every family's vrat vegetable list (assumption: common North Indian vrat rules)

ekadashi.reason: the dish has no grains or pulses, but skip onion, garlic and hing (compounded hing usually contains wheat or rice flour) as most Ekadashi observers do

jain.reason: skip onion, garlic and fresh ginger (root vegetables) and use dry ginger powder (sonth) and tomato; okra itself grows above ground and is allowed

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, light and high in fibre; keep salt moderate if eating it at sehri, and pair it with roti and dal or curd for a fuller meal
